nodes.scale: 433 pages · 163 CRUDs · 619 rules · 22 studio consoles · 27 schedulers

nodes.statement: No library doc covers localizing BUSINESS ROWS. 20-localization.md handles content-node localizedMap and form/label text; A had to invent a per-row `localized` jsonb column, a dedicated CRUD with one `<entity>Loc` SQL method per table, a `*Loc` naming convention on the screen payload and a client-side merge helper. Any two-locale project with user-maintained reference data hits this on day one.

No doc states the BALANCE REVERSAL obligation: when a module makes a quantity move in a direction nothing moved it before, it must enumerate every flow that reverses, cancels or partially undoes that movement. 10-database-management.md and 11-business-logic-dynamic-crud.md cover ledgers and soft-delete but not this. It cost A a silently broken rejection path that no existing assertion could have caught.

No doc says SEED DATA IS NOT EVIDENCE. 10-database-management.md and 26-orchestration-and-testing.md should carry the rule: a balance is verified by causing a movement and re-reading it; a rowset written from the spec will always agree with the spec. A shipped a reconciling ledger that no rule in the project wrote, and nine test rounds passed over it.

No doc says a SCREEN IS THE UNION OF ITS SCRIPTS, or that a defect-class sweep must enumerate `studioModel.scripts[]` programmatically. 24d-html-component-structure.md covers when to split a component but not that a fix anchored on the script named `main` misses exactly the components that have two — which in A was the dashboard and the biggest screen in the project.

No doc warns that an ASSERTION OVER A STRUCTURE MUST STATE WHAT IT EXPECTS TO FIND. A scan that returns empty reports success. Three separate A checks passed while the defect was live in front of them, one of them because a form page names its CRUD alias eight levels down in `properties.settings` rather than in `properties.model.stringValue` — a structural fact 06-form-groups-and-mapping.md does not surface.

24-html-component-studio.md §1.2 promises "if the component breaks, the boring page still runs the business", but nothing enforces it. A has 71 CRUD form actions with no `onBeforeCompleteRuleIdentifier` — validate WARNs, it does not ERROR — so the fallback layer is decorative for most entities. This should be an error, or the doc should stop making the promise.

No doc covers CROSS-CUTTING INSTRUMENTATION of the `ctx.callRule` bridge (wrap once, inject the reading locale, time the call, log info/error to a project table, guard against logging the logger, guard against double-wrapping on re-mount). A implemented it 19 times because there was no canonical recipe to vendor.

No doc covers the SELF-DIAGNOSIS CONSOLE pattern — `Identity Check`, `Locale Probe`, `Schema Migration Status` / `Apply Schema Migration` as in-app rules on a Logs page. In a tenant where the role API is fail-closed and the session locale does not follow the header switch, these are the only way an operator can distinguish a configuration problem from a code problem, and 28-support-mode-over-mcp.md would be the natural home.

17-left-nav-quick-links.md tells you not to put business pages in `Pages`, but `validate` does not FAIL on it. A nests the entire application inside the authoring drawer, duplicates Home as Dashboard, and makes every sub-heading a link to its first child — and only the last of those three raises a warning (11 times). The first two are silent.

No doc covers the CAPABILITY-FLAG CONTRACT between a studio screen and its rules: which flags a `<Screen> Rights` rule should return, that it must report `decidedBy`/`degraded` when the platform role API cannot resolve, and that the command rule re-checks server-side regardless. 16-groovy-service-api.md §2.3 documents that the API is fail-closed but not what to build on top of it.

24-html-component-studio.md §1.2 lists the costs you take on but does not tell you to BUILD THE SHARED KIT BEFORE THE SECOND COMPONENT. A's kit contains one feature; `errText` is duplicated 24 times, `applyLocale`/`say`/`bind`/`esc` 23 times. The doc should name the specific helper set (error formatting, message strip, event binding, escaping, locale swap, the action wrapper) as kit-from-the-start.

Nothing warns that all schedulers export `enabled: true` by default in practice — validate WARNs per scheduler (27 lines here) but the guidance to ship `enabled:false` and flip after import is buried. A project importing A cold starts a 5-minute watchdog and a financial period close the same night.

No library doc covers **graph/chain aggregation** — the party-level SUM across every branch and the frontier rule for "what is still recoverable". It is the single hardest piece of business logic in this project, its two failure modes (largest-branch reading, and double-counting every non-terminal hop) are both silent, and an integrator would have to rediscover them. Worth a short section wherever domain-logic recipes live (08 or a new one).

**Deadlines as data** is undocumented. A `deadline_policy` table (code / durationValue / durationUnit / escalationPoints / ownerRole / approvalState) plus a business-maintained holiday CRUD plus an `applyPolicy(code, from, holidays)` closure with a `WORKING_DAYS` branch and a loop guard is a complete, reusable subsystem that every regulated brief needs. Nothing in the library names it, so it gets reinvented — usually as `plusDays(3)`.

**Separation of duties at instance level** is absent. Doc 08 explains predicates and doc 25 explains validation, but neither states the rule this project encodes: role checks are not enough, the predicate must compare the current user against *both* the proposer and the case owner, must re-read state from the database rather than the submitted row, and must return false on every unknown. This is the control an auditor tests first.

Doc 22 is thorough on chart mechanics but silent on **board-set discipline** — one dashboard per numbered report requirement, a fixed 4-KPI + 6-7-chart skeleton, one shared filter bar per board, and the `hdr_<chartId>` label convention for titles. Without that, 87 charts is a pile; with it, it is eight owned products.

Doc 22 never mentions **KPI delta polarity**. Half the tiles here are metrics where rising is bad (open cases, net loss, overdue requests) and set `increasing:{color:red}` deliberately. The library's own KPI recipe uses the default colouring, which is wrong for that half of the metrics and reads as a green tick on a worsening number.

The **tabbed multi-CRUD console** recipe is not written down. `nct.tab.plugin` appears in the plugin catalog, but the load-bearing contract — `tabModel.items[i]` binds to child parsis node `i` **by order**, and each tab must contain exactly a filter form plus a crud table — is only discoverable by reading an export. So is the sibling decision of when a child entity is a *tab* (own filter, own actions, own export) versus a *line* (`insert_/delete_<lines>`).

Doc 08 does not warn that Groovy has **no include mechanism**, and gives no convention for the consequence. Here the helper prelude is copy-pasted up to 101 times and `applyPlaybook` — the closure whose own comment claims it is "the same headless closure" — physically exists three times. The library should either name a convention (keep the prelude byte-identical, generate it, list which rules carry it) or state plainly that shared logic belongs in a CRUD SQL method instead.

Nothing says an **export action must re-apply the find rule's row scope and audit itself**. Doc 04 covers row actions and doc 15 covers PDF rendering; the security consequence falls between them, and an export that bypasses scoping is a privilege-escalation route that passes every gate.

The gate ladder (validate → crud verify → pack → import → livediff) goes **green on a project whose entire process layer is inert**. All 8 workflows here are `deployed: false` and all 10 schedulers `enabled: false`, so five user-facing actions throw `workflow_is_not_deployed` at runtime and eight worklists render empty. `validate` does emit the warning, but it is one line among 91 and nothing in the handoff or delivery docs makes "deploy the workflows, enable the schedulers, name the service user" a required step.

Doc 22 §2.6 Rule 5 correctly forbids `now()`-anchored windows **in chart SQL**, but says nothing about the same problem in **dynamic-CRUD SQL methods**. Every `find*Candidates` / `find*AtRisk` / `find*Overdue` method here uses `now()`, which is right for a live system and returns nothing against the frozen `project-db.dump` — so the operational half of a demo is empty for a reason no one is warned about, and nothing tells the operator to re-date the seed.

Nothing warns about **template-inherited role group names surviving into the nav**. One quick link here is gated to five role groups that belong to an unrelated domain and do not exist in this project, so the home dashboard is invisible in the menu to every real role, and `validate` does not catch it. A check that every `roleGroupAccessors` key in the shared nav exists in `rep-objects.roleGroups[]` would be cheap and would also catch the six orphan queries and two UUID-named process groups in this export.

Doc 20 covers localization but not the failure seen here: a lookup query that builds a `VALUES (code, hy, ru, en, ord)` table with all three languages and then selects only `hy AS name`, so the dashboard filter bar is single-language while everything around it is trilingual. The pattern needed is "select the label column for the active locale", and it is not written anywhere.

`startedByRuleName` in a worklist column: docs 07 §provenance, 16 §2.12 and 27 say the platform stamps `startedByRuleIdentifier` / `startedByRuleName` / `startedByCrudAlias` and that they are "readable as context.data.startedByRuleName". That is true for a RULE but not for a process.table column — a `scope:GLOBAL` column reads `contextData.attrs`, where provenance never lands, so the column is blank on every row for ever. The docs should say plainly that provenance is rule-readable only, and that a worklist column showing it must be fed by an attr the start rule writes itself.

No doc covers "a threshold ladder is a register, not an if/else": the band table shape (code, value, `max_<x>` ceiling with NULL = open-ended top band, sort_order, active, description carrying the requirement clause) plus the `WHERE active AND (ceiling IS NULL OR :x <= ceiling) ORDER BY value ASC LIMIT 1` selector. This is the cleanest way to satisfy a PRD that says "configurable without a rebuild" and it appears nowhere in the library.

Effective-dated parameter registers are undocumented as a pattern: the `version` / `effective_from` / `DRAFT→ACTIVE→SUPERSEDED` triad, `nextVersion`, an `activate` that computes every derived quantity in SQL at activation time, `supersedeOthers`, the partial unique index on (entity_id, version) — and crucially the companion rule that documents must SNAPSHOT the parameters they were computed from onto their own line rows, or the versioning explains nothing later.

Doc 22 shows `date_trunc('month', min/max(col))` for building a period spine but never states the rule that a rolling dashboard window must be anchored on `MAX(data)` rather than `now()`. Every chart in a PoC, a demo tenant or a restored dump goes blank without it — this deserves to be a named rule in 22, together with generating the period-filter lookup from the identical expression.

Doc 10 mentions `WHERE deleted = false` indexes in passing but does not state the requirement: any human-facing document number (`po_no`, `receipt_no`, `claim_no`, …) on a soft-deleted table needs a PARTIAL unique index `… WHERE (deleted = false)`, or delete-and-recreate collides for ever. Likewise the companion decision — number generated inside the INSERT via `COALESCE(NULLIF(:no,''), 'PFX-'||to_char(now(),'YYMMDD')||'-'||<6 hex>)` — and its honest cost (random, so the unique index turns a collision into a failed insert).

The Postgres semantics that two of this project's CRUD methods depend on are stated nowhere: inside a single `UPDATE`, every column reference on the right-hand side sees the PRE-update value, so a derived column written in the same statement must repeat the whole expression rather than read the column being written. Belongs in 11 next to the mutator-method recipes.

No recipe for pro-rata allocation across lines in one statement — `UPDATE <lines> l SET share = extra * (l.qty / NULLIF(total,0)) FROM (SELECT header aggregate) h WHERE l.parent_id = h.id`. Landed cost, freight, discount and tax apportionment all have this shape and it is a two-line answer once seen.

Doc 27 stops at claim + repair. It does not cover the third member of the family: `endCase` — clearing both claim columns when the process ends on a branch — without which a subject that is reopened later (postponed → resumed) stays claimed for ever and never gets a fresh case. Nor does it cover the choice of releasing the claim from the branch rule itself versus from the repair sweep.

There is no "small project skeleton" anywhere in the library. Doc 13 is the empty→dynamic playbook and doc 19 is the decision procedure, but nothing states the target SHAPE of a ≤15-aggregate build: one context, one register/document page per aggregate, one BPMN, a handful of schedulers, one dashboard, form pages as children never nav entries — nor the naming grid that makes it navigable (`<noun>` / `<thing>-forms` / `form-<thing>` / `Find — X` / `Choices X` / `X Action Create|Update|Delete` / `X Is <Status>` / `Is <Role>`).

Idempotency by counting an append-only journal (`countByReference(reference_id, movement_type) > 0`) is not offered anywhere as an alternative to a `processed` flag, even though doc 27 devotes a section to idempotency for process starts. The same reasoning applies to any step reachable from both a row action and a service task.

Nothing documents the observed "action side-form" idiom or its failure mode as a *pattern with a correct form*. `validate` catches it (12 errors here), but the library has no positive recipe for "a small form that collects two extra fields for a row action": which scope to use, and how to write the rule when the same form is reachable from both a CRUD row action and a workflow task (attrs first, then the row).

A single-source-of-addresses rule (`Notification Recipients` returning a map, called by every mailing rule) is an obvious operational win after an import into a new environment — one rule to edit instead of eleven — and no doc suggests it.

Doc 17 never says what to DO with the `Pages` group itself — the 3/3 convention (keep it at order 0, put one `roleAccess` granting `Author` on the GROUP node) deserves to be a numbered step with the JSON, not a parenthetical inside Gotcha 8(c). It is the single highest-value nav edit in a build.

Doc 17 instructs that business groups go FIRST and Home be moved to the top of the sidebar; all three good projects instead left `Pages` at order 0 and gated it. Same rendered result, opposite literal instruction. The doc should name the decision and jump the way the projects jumped — gating is idempotent under re-running `quicklink add --group Pages` and does not renumber the baseline.

No doc and no `validate` rule covers `roleGroupAccessors` keys that name a role group the project does not have. Five phantom names (`Software Specialist`, `Front Office Employee`, `Diagnostic Technician`, `Diagnostic Head`, `Hardware Specialist`) shipped in 3/4 projects, in one case on C's own front-door quick link, making the cockpit invisible to every business persona.

Nothing warns that a naive localization pass translates `localizedMap.icon` VALUES into non-existent CSS classes. All four exports carry the identical corrupted baseline entries (`pe-7s գործիքներ`, `pe-7s-կրկնություն`, `pe-7s-խաղ`), so the console icons vanish under one locale in every project ever built from that baseline.

Nothing warns that a stale `localizedMap.icon` silently overrides a freshly-set `icon` — the reason one project's renamed cockpit link still renders a house instead of its chosen dashboard glyph. Renaming a nav link is four edits, not one.

Doc 17 documents `roleAccess` on a nav item but not the two mutually-exclusive schools of granting build identities (`accessors.admin/nct_author` vs `roleGroupAccessors.Author/Developer/<SysAdmin>`). Mixing them produces an item hidden from everyone, which no gate detects.

Doc 21 presents its two-rung ladder as a choice; in practice 4/4 took rung 1 and `Redirect` was used zero times. The doc should say so, and should give the tell for a GOOD rung 1 (~10 `nct.parsis.plugin` grid cells + a KPI strip + one `global.replacement.plugin`, seen in 3/4) rather than nine charts in a single parsis.

Doc 21 warns not to alias the root but not that generated documentation will invent one anyway — a delivered user manual printed `/<project>/home` as the address of the main screen, which 404s. Any README/manual emitted at closeout must render the front door as the bare project URL.

Neither doc gives a measurable reachability criterion. It becomes checkable as: unlinked depth-1 pages must be a subset of {Profile, Sources, Queries, Branches, Insights, Advisory, Ontology, reports, 401, 404} — an exact match in 3/3 good projects.

Neither doc states the depth rule (two levels: group → link, zero links carrying children in 3/3 good projects) nor the group-sizing range (1–9 links, median 4–6), nor that a group must be a `PageModel` with NO `linkModel` — the distinction A violated 12 times, 10 of them by pointing a 'folder' at its own first child.
Neither doc mentions the `form-` / `wl-` / `rpt-` alias namespaces that make 'is this page a nav target?' answerable from the alias alone (used in 3/3 good projects, absent entirely in the bad one).

Doc 17's Gotcha 1 gives per-page-node counts from `empty`; it should carry the field numbers instead — 755/755 per-page kickers across four shipped projects delegate to `23ab2aca-…`, and all 622 populated copies still hold the untouched factory stub (504 at 1512 chars, 118 at 1831) with its `Sourcese`/`Dashboars` typos. That is the argument that ends the discussion, and it also yields the only reliable success signal for a nav edit: the shared node's `modelGroups` byte length changing.

§6.1 states 'there is no shared palette object, and cssByTheme cannot reach inside the canvas', which pushes authors to paste hex literals into every chart. cssByTheme CAN carry a per-theme token table that JS reads back with getComputedStyle().getPropertyValue() — verified in 31 charts across 5 skins. The advice should become: paste the token table, read the tokens.

§3.2 documents query.parameters as 'a seed' but never warns that the editor persists the author's preview pick into the shipped node. Two of four projects shipped a board that opens pre-filtered, one of them to a named customer supplier — both a UX defect and a data-leak channel. Needs a ⛔ plus the pre-pack audit.

§5.2's warning that the clicked value must equal the DB value leaves the reader to invent the fix. The corpus's fix (bind a second String[] from a code column; colour and crossFilter on it, display the label) is used 26 times in one project and should be Recipe C's default shape, not a footnote.

Gotcha 16 offers three localization workarounds and its 'last resort: one chart node per language' is worse than a technique actually shipped: resolve the locale in the chart's own JS from ?lng= → ?lang= → `lang` cookie → <html lang>, then branch with L(en,hy) and translate DB enums with a WORDS map. It is the ONLY technique that reaches dataset labels, axis units, tooltip prefixes and empty states.

§2.3 documents the Full row shape as {cols:[{label:'<col>', value:<v>, …}]}. One deployment emits {cols:[{column:{name:'<col>',…}, <value>}]} with no `label` and the value under an undocumented key, and the payload can arrive as a JSON *string* so rows.length counts characters. The doc needs the asRows()/flattenRow() defensive pair, which handles all observed shapes.

§2B.5's bullet 'Title inside the chart, align:start' directly contradicts the same doc's Gotcha 16 and is used by only 2 of the 185 charts in the corpus, neither of them on a board. Following it makes the one string a reader needs permanently monolingual. It should be replaced by 'the title is a sibling nct.label.plugin with tagName: h6'.

§1.4 documents maxItemsCount and its 1000 default but never says to set it to 1 on a single-row KPI query — 17 of the corpus's KPI tiles do, and it is free insurance against a later GROUP BY silently turning one number into the first of many.

Recipe D / §6's Plotly snippet omits ResizeObserver, which §2B.4's KPI recipe includes. 17 of 49 Plotly tiles in the corpus omit it and never resize when their Bootstrap column does. There should be one canonical Plotly snippet and it should carry the observer.

Nothing in the doc mentions delta polarity: on a 'bad when it rises' metric the Plotly indicator's increasing/decreasing colours must be inverted, or half a risk board's tiles read backwards. One project does this deliberately.

§4.6 shows the Since lookup as a DISTINCT over one table. On a board charting several fact tables that silently offers periods some charts have no rows in; the working form UNIONs every charted fact table's date column, as one project does.

The doc gives no dataset-construction recipe for a stacked/grouped bar. Two working approaches exist and the choice matters: pivot in SQL with count(*) FILTER when the series set is fixed, pivot in JS from a long (key, series, value) triple with an explicit ORDER array when it is data-driven. §2B.4(d) only shows the options object.

futureReplacements / showFutureQuery is documented at length in §5.1 and is never used: the `futureReplacements` key is absent from all 185 chart models. The corpus's only drill mechanism is a plain window.location from the onClick handler. §5.1 should open by saying it is effectively dead and point straight at §5.3.

§1.2's worked example uses Utils.CHART_COLORS.red / Utils.transparentize — a platform template helper that appears only in legacy content (7 charts) and never in the three current projects, and which models exactly the no-explicit-colour-decision that §6.1 forbids.

The doc never states that <plugin id="…"> resolves on the child node's `identifier` — not its `id`, `uniqueIdentifier` or `name`. It is the most load-bearing detail of dashboard composition and all four projects depend on it; identifiers are free strings (hdr_<uuid>, h-r1c2, rop-kpi-3), which the doc also never says.

24a §6's list of legitimate per-skin `byTheme` uses (image / shadow / gradient / one-skin contrast rescue) omits the one category every project needs: the SEMANTIC STATUS RAMP. §4 correctly warns that hue does not carry state on the dark skins (Dracula --cyan==--pink==--purple, Dark Blue --green==--purple) but its only remedy is "pair a state colour with an icon or a word". The delivered answer is to stop using the platform's state tokens for state and declare your own, with four byte-identical dark blocks — 755 B per key, ~150 B of it declarations.

24a §8 and 24d §4 both instruct "one CSS prefix per component" / "rename `cmp-` per component". Followed literally that produced 26 copies of one kit across 22 components, 540 KB, 107 lines byte-identical in every file and 120 of 940 selectors shared by 20+, and four screens still carrying a second obsolete kit. The rule should be one kit prefix per PROJECT plus a short per-screen prefix for what is unique — and the doc never mentions that `studioModel.libs[].assets[].kind` accepts `"CSS"`, which is the mechanism for shipping that kit once (with the honest caveat that a CSS lib asset is page-global and unscoped).

No library doc describes the composition family at all — the zero-authored-CSS console that 3 of 4 delivered projects are made of. `main-card mb-3 card` + one `icon-gradient bg-*` + `lnr-*` + `card-header` label plugin + `row g-4` + `col-12 col-lg-*` + `nct.parsis.plugin` per cell + `card-body py-2 px-3` for density + `he-100` for equal heights, with the ~1:1:1 html:label:slot node ratio as the tell. 14/14a catalogue the plugins; nothing teaches the layout grammar.

24a §9 cannot see an undefined custom property. `var(--app-ink)` with no fallback invalidates the entire declaration, the control renders unstyled, nothing logs and validate is green. It is the exact failure the token approach the doc recommends makes possible, and it needs a named gate (~25 lines) beside the §9.2 greps.

24a §3.2's token contract has no entry for `opacity`, which is strictly better than a muted-colour token for de-emphasised text (no token, no fallback, cannot go out of contrast range), and no entry for `rgba(127,127,127,.10–.28)`, which all four projects invented independently and is the only theme-safe neutral available inside chart JS where CSS variables are unreachable.

24a §8's starter kit pairs `color-mix()` with nothing. On a browser without color-mix the focus ring disappears entirely — an accessibility regression. The delivered form is two declarations, rgba first, color-mix second, at a cost of 40 bytes. The kit also sets `font-family` on the root class; every one of the 22 delivered consoles did the same and each therefore renders in a different typeface from the breadcrumb directly above it.

24 §4.4 lists empty/loading/error states as "cost you take on" and gives no vocabulary. The delivered answer is one slot and four sentences — `Loading…` authored into the markup so the first paint is never blank, a specific empty sentence, `Could not load <thing>: ` + server message, and an outer try/catch that writes `Script error: …` into the same slot. Plus: `classList` never `className` on the message strip, empty-message-hides, clear-before / re-assert-after, one module-level busy flag, em dash never zero.

24 §7 documents the `ctx.breadcrumb` API but not how to adopt it without rewriting every screen. The DOM-proxy technique (hide the source button rather than remove it, MutationObserver on disabled/hidden/title, ancestor `[hidden]` check, resolve the spinner on the FIRST disabled-mutation rather than by re-reading the final state) is ~150 lines and is what let 20 of 22 consoles keep their own action logic.

22 §6 has no chart container scale and no ramp naming. The delivered numbers: 92–150px for a KPI indicator, 280–340px for a panel chart, 360–440px for a feature chart; `position:relative` + a fixed pixel height plus `maintainAspectRatio:false` on every Chart.js instance; `calc(100% - 1.9rem)` to reserve an in-container title. And four ramps named by role — categorical `--c1…c8`, semantic `--c-good/warn/risk/crit/mute`, sequential `--r1…r4`, diverging `--div-up/--div-down` — declared in cssByTheme and read back with getComputedStyle, so a new skin never touches the js.

Nothing in the library states the interaction semantics these projects had to learn in production: primary colour means "this acts" (selection is a segmented/pressed treatment, not an accent fill); a disclosure must name what it opened and never share a caption with the control that acts; a disabled control is the worse copy of a server rule that already refuses; a field that cannot be computed states why in the space it occupies rather than disappearing; and a class applied for a visual effect is checked against the stylesheet that is supposed to give it one.

A contradiction the integrator must settle: three projects put a `dynaform.filter.form.plugin` in the same slot above every `crud.table.plugin` (31 + 33 + 12 occurrences); the A shipped 129 bare tables with no filter bar. Jump the filter-form way — a table with no filter bar forces column-header filtering, which is discoverable only if you already know it is there.

A second open decision no project settles: every studio console renders its own `<h1>` while sitting directly under a breadcrumb that already names the page — two page titles ~30px apart. Decide once whether the h1 earns its place (it does when it carries a subtitle or a live status pill) or whether the screen should start at the KPI strip.

Accessibility gap present in all 22 delivered consoles despite a WCAG 2.1 AA requirement in the PRD: `aria-pressed` is used 87 times and `aria-label` on every unlabelled input, but `aria-live` appears ZERO times — the message strip that carries every success and every refusal is never announced. One attribute.

Doc 01 documents `accessors` as "access by system roles" but never says the authoring dialog writes one of only two fixed 27-key stanzas, that the business-page default grants view:true to twelve of them (user_*, role_group_*, file_storage_*), or that the check is disjunctive with roleGroupAccessors — so a persona holding FILE_STORAGE_VIEW defeats every persona gate. This is the single largest doc gap; it needs the stanza JSON, the intersection check, and the instruction to force the stanza down to admin/nct_author on restricted pages.

Nothing in the library connects `rep-objects.roleGroups[].roles[]` (uppercase platform roles) to the lowercase keys of a node's `accessors` map. Doc 12 §4.4 validates the constants; doc 01 lists the accessor keys; neither says they are the same set, which is what makes the bypass invisible.

Doc 19 Phase 6 gives the row-scope recipe as `filter['ownerEmail'] = service.security.user().email`, i.e. own-rows only. It has no shape for ORG-UNIT scope, which needs an identity→scope lookup table and, critically, a fail-closed sentinel of the column's own type: the generated SQL idiom `COALESCE(CAST(NULLIF(CAST(:p AS text),'') AS uuid), col)` reads an empty string as "no filter", so the obvious `return ''` on lookup failure returns the entire table.

Doc 04 scopes the table and mentions the column projection, but nothing tells the integrator that the same scope must be repeated on the RIMM_* choices rule, the export rule, and any purpose-built list method — nor how to scope a child table that has no scope column (subquery on the parent, with the scope as a declared SQL parameter).

Charts are undocumented as a security surface. Doc 22 never says a chart query cannot see the current user, so a row-scoped project ships an unscoped dashboard. The doc needs the three options (gate the dashboard page/chart node to the oversight personas, pass a scope parameter and accept it is a filter, or build the tile in an HTML component over a scoped rule) and an instruction to decide in Phase 6.

Doc 17 says a nav item's roleAccess is checked like a node's, but not the two ways it dies in practice: leaving publicReadAccess:true makes the whole map inert (the check short-circuits before any group is read), and a grant to a role-group name that is not in rep-objects.roleGroups is a grant that can never match — present on the Home/Users links in 3 of 4 projects, hiding the home page from every real user, with nothing in validate, pack or import reporting it.

`mrjun.py validate` covers canonical ReportRole values and dangling scheduler/form-group predicates, but has no security checks at all for: hasAnyRoleGroup("X") string literals that match no role group; roleGroupAccessors / nav-item keys that match no role group; publicReadAccess:true beside a group grant; edit:true with view:false; a role group with zero userRoleGroupAssignments; a persona-gated page whose accessors stanza grants a role that persona holds; a write action with no predicateIdentifier; a scoped fetch rule whose key is not declared in both findAll and count. All of these found real defects here.

Doc 16 §2.10 documents service.rule("Name") for reuse, but the library never resolves the fork it creates for security: inline the role list in each predicate (one project repeats the same six-name oversight list 30 times) or factor it into `Is <Persona>` rules and compose. The guidance should be: compose the role half, inline the state half — and warn that putting the state assertion inside the shared four-eyes rule broke every Reverse button on nine document types in one project.

Doc 12 §3.2 notes serviceUserId affects service.security in a scheduler, but does not draw the conclusion that a scoped fetch rule reused from a scheduler returns zero rows for ever (it takes the !hasAnyRoleGroup branch and the fail-closed sentinel). The rule to state is: share the SQL method between the screen and the sweep, never the scoped wrapper.

No doc names the naming/sizing conventions the four projects converge on: exactly two authoring groups called Author and Developer (Developer = Author + ADMIN), one group per PRD actor named after the job, and — the one genuinely good project-specific idea — a separate customer-side `System Administrator` group appended to every predicate's role list so the customer can unblock their own users without the integrator's account.

The three-tier permission convention for roleGroupAccessors (authoring = view+edit+advancedEdit, working persona = view+edit, oversight = view only) is followed by 967 grants but appears in no doc, and neither does the corollary that `edit:true` with `view:false` grants nothing because the render check reads `view`.

Doc 01 warns that admin bypasses roleAccess, and doc 16 that hasAnyRoleGroup is fail-closed, but neither states the practical rule that follows: you need one no-role test account per persona, because Author/Developer/System Administrator all hold ADMIN and one project's rule comments claim hasAnyRoleGroup answers true for any name for an ADMIN/NCT_AUTHOR account — so authoring accounts can test none of the four layers.

INSERT … ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING RETURNING * is a second atomic idempotency primitive and appears nowhere in the library — doc 27 §5.3 offers only the UPDATE claim. It needs its three specifics documented: a PARTIAL unique index (WHERE deleted=false), an explicit deleted=false in the INSERT so the row falls inside that index, and returnsArray:false so 'already there' comes back as Groovy null.

Doc 07's 'three start shapes' presents a start form (A/B) as normal. Across four delivered projects: shape A 0 times, shape B 0 times, shape C (a rule) 15 times, and userStartProcessActions empty on 14 of 14 worklists. The library should invert the default.

The claim layout doc 27 §5.3 prescribes (a state transition) cannot be repaired by age. The strongest project uses a separate process_started_at / process_identifier / process_start_count triple precisely so findClaimedWithoutCase can key on a 5-minute age, and makes the gate's count* query count the repairable backlog so the schedule wakes for it. Neither the triple nor the age-based repair query is in the library.

Nothing says 'release the claim on a terminal branch that allows re-entry'. A case ending on a postpone/park branch leaves its subject claimed for ever unless that branch's complete rule clears the claim columns — a silent, permanent stall the corpus hit and fixed with an endCase method.

Nothing says 'a sweep must not write a field a running case's gateway routes on'. service.workflow has no cancel/complete, so the mistake is unrecoverable from a rule. Sweeps must write annotation columns only; the case writes state.
Repair-before-sweep ordering is unmentioned: running the repair at the TOP of the case-opening rule hands a crashed tick's claim back in time for the SAME pass, instead of the next one.

Doc 27 §6 insists localeKey be read off the claimed row and never a literal. The corpus shows three valid sources (session locale, a literal, omitted) and shows that per-language mail templates chosen by a recipient lookup beat a case-level localeKey whenever one case writes to several people in different languages.

Doc 07 Rule 1 says a task form showing an existing record must be all-GLOBAL. One project made 100 %-CRUD-scope task forms work with an onBeforeUserTaskStartRuleIdentifier loader that both PUTs the row into the crud map and RETURNS it. The library should name this as the sanctioned exception with its never-throw discipline. It should also state the positive half the corpus proves: CRUD scope in a task form is correct when the step CREATES.
'The gate is the candidate query with LIMIT 1' (10 of 16 gated schedules) should be the documented default gate recipe — it is the only shape in which the gate cannot drift from the action.

validate blind spot found in real data: a PREDICATE whose COMMENT contains the words service.workflow.start — written precisely to explain that it is forbidden there — will trip a naive 'start inside a predicate' scan. The contextDataMap check strips comments first; this one should too.

service.workflow.list is never called, in any project, for anything. If the library keeps offering it as an idempotency option it should say plainly that no delivered project chose it; the claim column won every time.

job.explanation is used by three projects as the design record (why this cron, where the deadline lives, what the gate is) — the library treats it as a label. Doc 12 §3.1 should call for that sentence.

Doc 27 §2.0 nominates a service task for 'one process starts another'; the corpus does it from a user ACTION's onBeforeUserTaskCompleteRuleIdentifier, which is precise to the branch a human chose and can refuse in the same rule.

No guidance exists on WHICH branch a gateway's default should point at. Because a predicate answers false for every reason it could not decide, the default is 'where the process lands when it could not tell' and must be the reversible branch — two projects get this right and one points default at 'raise the follow-up document' and 'post the movement'.

Nothing gives a mechanical check for the inert-workflow defect. Grepping each workflows[].identifier across the unpacked export and expecting ≥3 hits (definition + node model + settings mirror) catches it instantly; the biggest project in the corpus shipped five workflows at exactly one hit each.

<bpmndi:BPMNLabel> for branch names is treated only as a hazard (the XSD ordering trap). Eight diagrams in the corpus name every branch and position none, so the canvas shows bare arrows out of every diamond — the label bounds are half the job, not an optional extra.

`forms[].hiddenConfigs` (Hidden Content Configuration) has 0 uses in 228 forms — the doc gives it a first-class panel; four teams instead forked the form into an 'approval twin' with `alwaysProhibited:true`. Demote it and point at the fork.

The 51-template `conditionalValidations` catalog has 3 uses in 2,119 controls, and 2 of the 3 ignore the generated §2.2 preamble in favour of a `try { v } / fallback` read. The catalog is mis-weighted: doc 25 should lead with `alwaysMandatory` + form-level `validators`.

`service.actionId == '<uuid>'` mapping-predicate forks: 0 uses in four projects. All six live forks route on row state + role. The doc should lead with the state/role fork and demote the actionId idiom (which is uuid-coupled and unbound on workflow branches).

The 'Create Validation from Template' dialog copies the default-locale message into every locale — the one live generated validation shipped default-locale placeholder text ('Value does not match the required pattern') to the users of both other locales. Undocumented.

Bare `addFieldError` / `addError` / `addFieldWarning` (unqualified, no `validation.` prefix) resolve at runtime — 32 live calls gating 14 document forms. Docs 25 and 02 present only the `validation.*` spelling.

A *computed* validation message has no localization mechanism; projects hand-roll `def loc = service.global.locale.getKey() ?: '<default>'` plus a `[key: [locale: text]]` map. That idiom belongs in doc 25 §4.2.

`context.currentData?.getField('<field>', <Type>.class)` is the fallback read for a validation predicate on a control inside a list-item sub-form. Doc 02 mentions `context.currentData.get()` only in passing; the `getField` form is what a real rule uses.

`attrs.get('_crudEntityId')` — the row id the platform threads on the CRUD-table path — is used by every predicate and rule in one project and appears in no doc. It is the middle leg of the three-way row-id resolver that makes a rule work from both a table row action and a workflow task.

`formModeIdentifier` may live on the `dynaform.form.plugin` node instead of the `siteMapPage` (141 of 142 forms in one project do exactly that). The doc calls the page property mandatory; the truthful statement is 'somewhere in the page subtree — write both'.

`placeFormsNextToLanding` is advisory once the pages exist: one project ships `false` on all 145 groups while 103 of its 142 form pages are siblings of their landing, and it runs. The doc reads as if the flag describes the shipped tree.

The action-icon list in doc 06 omits more than half the icons in real use: pe-7s-edit (123 uses), pe-7s-look (30, the read-only View convention), pe-7s-close-circle (25, reject), pe-7s-cloud-download (19, export), pe-7s-print, pe-7s-back (reverse), pe-7s-power (close), pe-7s-play, pe-7s-up-arrow, pe-7s-shield, pe-7s-lock, pe-7s-clock, pe-7s-shuffle, pe-7s-less, pe-7s-box2.

`localizedButtonNames` is documented as 'the submit label'; in practice five name→button pairs recur as a UX convention — View→Back (27), Open→Close, Edit→Save (21), Add/Create→Save (102), Export→Run (19).

The '63-key authoritative settings union' in doc 02 is field-controls-only: `dynaform.filter.submit.button.plugin` carries `buttonName` and `waitComponentIdentifier` on 95 live nodes, and the doc claims the union is the only set of keys that can appear in `settings.stringValue`.

`between:true` is presented as a rare exotic mode assembled from classes; all 21 live uses are the standard date-range FILTER control (`filterKey:<x>From` + `betweenMapping.filterKey:<x>To`, `scope:GLOBAL`, LocalDate picker) and none are on a data-entry form.

The List sub-form action block is a fixed template that 22 of 22 live List controls reproduce byte-identically (Add/Edit/Delete; `direct` as the STRING "off"/"on"; `formIdByActionId` folding Edit onto the Create sub-form; one child `dynaform.list.item.plugin` whose identifier IS the Create action id; `localizedHeaderLabel` + `headerIcon:"pe-7s-list"`). Doc 02 §7/§8 gives the mechanism but not the template.

The worklist combination `direct:"off"` + `submitForm:false` + `completeUserTask:"off"` + `formInModal:true` — read the subject in a dialog without claiming or completing the task — is not described anywhere.

Unknown keys inside `properties.model` / `properties.settings` survive the export round-trip: one project stashes generator provenance on its actions (`lifeAlias`, `printAlias`, `v12Alias`, `digestAlias`) and one leaks a `__children__` node blob into a List control's settings. The deserializer drops them but they persist in JSON and vanish the moment a human edits that panel — worth an explicit warning.

doc 11 says sourcePassword is 'in plaintext in the export' and instructs you to 'fill in all 8 fields' — it is null in 244/244 CRUDs and 5/5 sources; the export scrubs it and import re-binds from sources[]. Writing a password into an export is both wrong and a credential leak.

doc 11 and doc 18 §3 both state a document `delete` MUST cascade to its lines (validate warns). All 19 documents in the corpus deliberately keep the lines, one with an explicit comment: the header is SOFT-deleted, so cascading would make `undelete` restore an empty shell. The rule is conditional — cascade on hard delete, keep on soft.

The read-only REPORT CRUD is undocumented and is 12 of 244: find + findAll + count only, no table behind it, findAll an inline UNION/aggregate query, and count = `SELECT COUNT(*) AS total FROM (<the whole findAll minus ORDER BY/LIMIT/OFFSET>) rpt`. Also undocumented: the utility/service CRUD (a bag of named SQL reads, no CRUD verbs).

Nothing in the library mentions that Postgres folds UNQUOTED SELECT aliases to lower case. 208 unquoted camelCase `<ref>__<col>` aliases ship in two projects, and one of them binds `fieldExpression: "case.name"` against a wire key that is actually `case`. The rule `AS "<ref>__<col>"` when either part has an upper-case letter is missing and is a silent-blank-column generator.

doc 11 frames the single-parameter `count` trap as 'the DEFAULT shape of count on any table with exactly one filter'. It occurs 0 times in 244 CRUDs, because real projects declare either no filters or two or more. The useful form of the advice is a design rule ('never ship a CRUD with exactly one filter'), not a runtime warning.

doc 11 §Gotchas frames a PARTIAL caller filter map as the trap. 96 of 96 rule call-sites in one project pass partial maps and work fine — because every predicate is text-anchored with NULLIF(:x,''). The doc under-states that the ANCHOR is the load-bearing defence and the caller-side seeding is secondary; and where seeding is used it is with '' (setString arm), never null.
doc 11 says returnsArray is 'true for findAll, false for the rest'. 60 non-findAll methods across three projects are true. Set it by result shape.
doc 18 §3's tree recipe still spells `:parentId::uuid`; the postfix `::` cast appears 0 times in 2115 methods — all four projects use `CAST(NULLIF(:x,'') AS uuid)` exclusively.

doc 18 §1's enum-lookup FK rules (`x_id = (SELECT id FROM lookup_x WHERE code = :x)`, `elN` join alias) appear 0 times. Every enum in the corpus is a CHECK-constrained varchar, and the shared vocabulary is factored into ONE `ref_label(vocabulary, code, label, localized, sort_order)` CRUD rather than N lookup CRUDs — a pattern the library never names.
doc 11 warns that `get` 'can lag' findAll. In 232/232 CRUDs the two SELECT lists are byte-identical. This deserves promotion from hazard to invariant with a one-line gate.

No doc states that `filterFields.fieldName == displayName` (487/487, always the camelCase parameter name) while `dtoFields.displayName` is the snake column — the two arrays use displayName for different things, and a mismatch in either is a reliable typo signal.

No doc states that the soft-delete flag must be kept OUT of dtoFields (0 of 81 CRUDs exposes `deleted`), nor that audit timestamps must be stamped with now() in SQL rather than declared as writable parameters (the one project that parameterised them has 160 CRUDs whose updated_at can never change).

The `parameterType` field is treated by the library as meaningful; in practice it is metadata only — one project declares Instant/Boolean/Integer/BigDecimal on 223 parameters whose SQL then anchors them as text, and it works. Also, `ObjectNode` occurs as a parameterType (10 times) and is not in the documented mapParamType output set.

Three methods in the corpus are syntactically broken SQL (`FROM item_parameterWHERE`, `now()WHERE` twice). No offline gate in the library looks for glued keywords, yet a one-line regex `[A-Za-z0-9_)'"](WHERE|FROM|SET |RETURNING|JOIN)\b` finds all three; only `crud verify --db` would otherwise catch them.

24 §4.4 lists two error envelopes (`{ok:false,error}` and the serialization failure) but not the third and most confusing one: a rule that throws returns `{"ok":false,"error":"[…ExecuteResponse$ExecutionError@33872ff2]"}` — the `error` field is present and its CONTENTS are a Java identity hash, so a faithful `e.message` renders a memory address as an explanation. The doc needs the shape and the /ExecutionError|ExecuteResponse\$|@[0-9a-f]{6,}/ test.

24d §3.5 and §10 state flatly that two scripts declaring the same top-level `const` produce `[Dokie] compile error` and kill the whole program. Both multi-script components in the study declare `const BOUND`, `esc`, `errText`, `L` (and in one case `const q`, `let TASKS`) in BOTH scripts and work, because each script is wrapped in its own top-level `try {}` block. The doc should document the try-block wrapper as the sanctioned way to keep scripts independent — and state its cost (script 2 cannot see script 1's helpers, so shared code must go in the lib or ctx.api).

Nothing in 24 or 24c describes per-source failure isolation in a fetch rule. The `def safe = { cl -> try { cl() ?: [] } catch (t) { __trace << …; [] } }` closure plus a `trace[]` field in the envelope is what makes a screen that fuses eight entities survivable, and it belongs beside 24 §4.4's error handling.

24 §4.4 prescribes a `paint()` macrotask yield before every blocking bridge call. In practice, authoring `Loading…` into `properties.html` makes the yield unnecessary for the first load (the server already painted it), which is why 21 of 22 components carry no paint() helper. The doc should name the markup-first loading state as the primary technique and the yield as the fallback for re-fetches.

24 §6.3's "register ctx.on/ctx.onCleanup before the first await" is presented as a discipline. The structural answer the projects found — keep the whole script body synchronous and launch the work as `load().catch(...)`, never awaited — makes the rule automatic and should be the doc's recommended shape.

24c is written entirely for server-side paging, but zero of the 22 components page on the server, deliberately: the bridge is a blocking XHR, so every page-turn/sort/filter would freeze the tab. The doc needs an explicit decision table (client-page under ~2 000 rows with the `rowsInPage` ceiling in the rule; server-page above it) rather than presenting server paging as the only contract.

24 §8 documents three wait mechanisms (icon-wait attributes, breadcrumb `wait`, ctx.busy). Across 3 047 html nodes and 22 components there are ZERO uses of any of them: busy is `btn.disabled = true` in a try/finally, which is also the signal the breadcrumb proxy observes. The doc should acknowledge the button-disable idiom as the default and scope ctx.busy to work with no button.

24 §7 covers declaring breadcrumb buttons but not the far cheaper proxy pattern (mirror an existing in-page button, forward click(), track label/disabled/hidden with a MutationObserver, resolve the spinner on the first `disabled` mutation). The spinner-resolution subtlety in particular is undocumented and is exactly where a naive implementation leaves a blockUI overlay up for 30 s.

24 §10 documents vendoring a third-party library but not vendoring YOUR OWN project kit — which is the highest-leverage use of libs[] and the thing that would have prevented ~4 400 lines of duplicated preamble in the one project that did reach for the studio.

24a §6 lists four legitimate reasons for a per-skin block; the study found the common fifth and it is not there: the platform's semantic tokens collapse to a single hue on Dracula (green==cyan==purple) and Dark Blue (green==purple), so a status palette bound to them stops carrying state. The remedy — define your own --<pfx>-ok/-warn/-bad aliases in "*" and re-declare only those lines in each dark key — deserves to be the doc's worked answer rather than a reader's inference from §4.

24a does not say that an `@media print` block inside css.byTheme cannot hide the application shell: the scoper prefixes every selector with #dokie-plug-<id> and rewrites a leading body/html/:root onto the wrapper, so you can only hide things inside your own component. The two working escapes (accept the chrome, or window.open('')+document.write+print) should be stated.

24 §5 and §9a describe ctx.contextData and the client/server permission split, but in practice ctx.contextData, ctx.bus, ctx.on, ctx.emit, ctx.byName, ctx.api, ctx.include, ctx.showHtml and ctx.setHtml are used ZERO times across all 22 components. The real ctx surface in production is ctx.root, ctx.callRule, ctx.onCleanup, ctx.libs and ctx.breadcrumb. A short "what you will actually use" table would set expectations correctly.

24 §4.4 tells you to gate the node with roleAccess AND the rule; all 22 components ship `publicReadAccess: true` and gate only in the rule. The doc should add the second consequence of a public studio node that has nothing to do with security: 24a §1.4's skin resolution reads the USER value only, so a public component renders as `Dark` for anonymous viewers regardless of the tenant.

No library doc covers the base64-through-ctx.callRule attachment round trip (FileReader → dataB64 → jsonb column → atob → Uint8Array → Blob → object URL), which is the only upload path available to a studio component because a rule has no upload API. It also needs the warning that the blocking bridge freezes the tab for the whole upload, so the size cap is not optional.

`mrjun.py validate` has no check for the two structural defects this study found most often: a `libNames: []` script that reads ctx.libs.<name> (works only via the empty-union fallback, and breaks silently the moment a second script declares any lib — 6 of 22 components rely on this), and a studio component whose script exceeds any sane size (median 42 kB, max 120 kB in one node, against 24d's ~200-line budget).

nct.html.plugin is a second, larger chart-shaped dead zone doc 20 never names: its `html` property is propertyType STRING with a permanently empty localizedStringValue, and there are 15x more html nodes than charts (1304/962/574/207 vs 55/31/87/12). The escape hatch (inline <plugin> + <prop type="LOCALIZED_STRING">, used 208 times by C) belongs in §iv beside the chart workarounds.

Groovy-returned user-facing text (rule return maps, validation.addError/addWarning, thrown messages) has NO per-locale slot anywhere in the export and is not listed as a dead zone, yet it is the largest body of user-visible text after labels. The MSG[loc] bank over service.global.locale.getKey() should be the documented answer.

Doc 20 §iv workaround 3 asserts ctx.callRule runs the rule with the viewer's session locale. A's authors observed the opposite and wrote a client-side __loc bridge across 17 screens, with the reason in a code comment: "the server decides its language from the session locale, which does not follow the header switch." The doc should qualify the claim or document the bridge.

localizationField spelling is documented as "either `localized` or `localize`"; in the wild it is `localized`, 3/3 of the projects that use it. Undocumented and load-bearing: the column must ALSO be declared as a dtoFields[] entry with fieldType "ObjectNode" — A has 6 CRUDs where the pointer is set and the field is absent, dead config the executor cannot use.

Doc 20 says a multilingual CHECK vocabulary must be "promoted to a small `localized` lookup table + a choices rule". C's 32 inline-literal ENUM_* rules (a Groovy rows list with a synthetic localize:[label:[...]] map) achieve the same with no table, no migration and no seed data. This cheaper answer is undocumented and should be the default for CHECK vocabularies.

The `localize` (Groovy/wire key) vs `localized` (DB column) split is stated but easy to invert. It deserves a one-line rule next to toSelectOptionsLocalized: Groovy always sees `localize`, SQL always sees the project's column spelling. Inverting it yields a dropdown that silently shows the base column.

The SQL access idiom COALESCE(t.localized->'<camelCaseField>'->>'<locale>', t.<base_column>, '<literal>') appears nowhere in the library, yet it is the only way a query, a chart replacement or a report reads localized data. All three C uses hard-code 'hy_AM', which is exactly why chart category labels stay monolingual — doc 20 §iv workaround 2 and doc 22 should carry the idiom plus a "pass the locale as a filter-bar parameter" recipe, since nobody in four projects built it.

Doc 20's "same string in every locale" warning has two legitimate exceptions it does not name (localizedMap.icon, deliberate blank spacers), and the inverse defect ships in all four projects: the platform's own seeded nav has machine-translated icon class names (pe-7s-օգտատերեր), so those items render no icon under hy/ru. The rule "never put a non-prose value where auto-translate can reach it" needs stating.

orInitLocalizedNames / orInitLocalizedButtonNames (byte-identical shadow copies of the two action maps, present only in the rep-objects.json CrudTable mirror; A 118, D 22, B and C none) appear in no library doc. The export-key inventory lists localizedLabels, defaultValueLocalized and infoText, none of which occur even once across four real projects (localizedHeaderLabel occurs 22 times total). Ordering the inventory by observed frequency, with unused rows marked, would be more useful.

Doc 20 does not warn that a hand-seeded localize jsonb in the WRONG shape imports cleanly and fails silently. B's 176 rows of flat {"en_US":"…","ru_RU":"…"} look 100% filled in the dump and render monolingually. A three-part gate — camelCase field key, full locale key, default slot equals base column — belongs in the checklist.

Doc 20's rule that a single-language project should author none of the machinery has a mirror-image case it does not cover: a MULTI-language project should still set multiLanguage:false on forms with no localized control. C is the only project that does (30 of 38); B, A and D render locale switchers on 27, 109 and 16 forms that switch nothing.

Doc 20 says nothing about WHICH entities deserve L3. Across all four projects every `localized` jsonb sits on a reference/dimension table (non-working day, reason code, organisational unit, item, location, process stage) and not one transaction table is localized. "Localize the dimension, never the fact" is a 4/4 convention worth stating, alongside "prose only — never a number, code, date or FK" (A localized a measured area, a measured temperature and an FK integer).

There is no cost model anywhere for the third language. One trilingual C screen (132 nodes) carries 91 per-locale maps of 8 distinct kinds ≈ 273 authored strings, none of which auto-fill on import. Doc 19's Phase-0 language elicitation would be much stronger with that number attached.
